Stem 5 to 15 cm, beige to brown, swollen, covered with a fine net that often runs down to the base
Thick white flesh, a little less firm than in the other ceps, yellowing with age; pleasant smell
In broadleaf woods, mostly under oaks; from May to November, after hot, damp weather

resources.string: Edible: it is on the German mycological society list (2026) and on the Swiss controllers’ list (2023). It lacks the pinkish flesh under the cap skin seen in the porcino, and its net runs further down (Wikipedia fr). The bitter bolete, which is inedible, has a coarser, darker net.

string-array.name: myco_proxima_traits
string-array.item: White cap, slightly ochre at the centre; more slender than the bearded amanita
White gills · white spores
White stem, with a membranous ring that stays
Large sac-like volva, rusty ochre: this is what sets it apart from the bearded amanita, whose volva is little or not coloured
In woods and at their edges, mostly under oaks on limy soil; in autumn; mostly around the Mediterranean

resources.string: Poisonous: it can cause serious kidney injury, sometimes requiring dialysis. It closely resembles Amanita ovoidea; volva colour alone cannot separate them safely. Suspected ingestion needs urgent medical advice. The exact toxin has not been established for this species.

string-array.name: myco_bisporus_traits
string-array.item: Wild form: cap 5 to 10 cm, pale grey-brown, with broad flat scales (the cultivated form is white)
Gills free and crowded: pink, then red-brown, then dark brown: never white
Thick, narrow ring, sometimes streaked above
Cylindrical stem up to 6 cm, no bulb or volva
Firm white flesh that turns pale pinkish-red when bruised
Rich soil, compost, manure, outside forests

resources.string: Edible: it is the most cultivated mushroom in the world, and it is on the DGfM and VAPKO lists. In the wild it is rare. It is confused with look-alikes that can be deadly: destroying angels (a volva at the base, pure white gills) and the toxic yellow stainer (phenol smell, flesh turning yellow). A mushroom growing on polluted ground can accumulate heavy metals.

string-array.name: myco_impudicus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 2 to 4 cm tall, conical and pitted, covered with olive-green to blackish slime
Stem 10 to 20 cm, white, pitted, hollow and fragile
Sac-like volva at the base: what remains of the burst egg
Foul carrion smell, noticeable from several metres
Young stage: a whitish egg of about 3 to 6 cm, with a layer of jelly
Broadleaf and conifer woods, near old stumps · late spring to autumn

resources.string: Edible only as a young egg, according to the DGfM list. Cut every egg in two: the egg of a deadly amanita already shows its cap and gills in a sac (see the death cap egg), a stinkhorn egg shows jelly around a white core. Once it has opened, the smell rules out any use.

string-array.name: myco_erinaceus_traits
string-array.item: One hanging mass, 10 to 20 cm, with no cap and no stem, fixed to the wood by a thick base
Soft, unbranched spines 2 to 7 cm long, hanging in tight rows
White when fresh, yellow-brown to reddish-brown as it dries
Soft, thick, white flesh that does not change
White spore print
Living or recently cut hardwood, mostly beech and oak · late summer and autumn

resources.string: Edible when young, according to the DGfM list and to Wikipedia, but it can be tough. It is rare: the DGfM marks it with category 2 of the German red list, and Wikipedia (en) says it is red-listed in several European countries. Close species also have spines on wood: Hericium coralloides and H. americanum.

string-array.name: myco_lignyotus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 8 cm, dark bistre-brown, matt and velvety, not zoned, with a small boss
Gills white, decurrent and forked, turning pale ochre; they redden where hurt
Stem the colour of the cap, narrowed and pleated, even pitted, at the top
White, watery milk that slowly turns brick-coloured on the flesh
White flesh that reddens a little in the air; weak smell and taste
Acid soils in the mid mountains, in fir woods · autumn

resources.string: Edible, according to the DGfM and VAPKO lists, and to Wikipedia (fr), which finds it tastier than the saffron milk cap. It is on the German red list (category 3). To tell it from Lactarius picinus and L. fuliginosus, whose gills are more yellow, look for the dark brown cap against white gills and the pleated top of the stem.

string-array.name: myco_turpis_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 20 cm, olive-brown to yellow-green, sticky in the centre; margin rolled in and shaggy when young
Dished at first, funnel-shaped with age, darkening to blackish
Gills crowded, dirty white, slightly decurrent; olive-brown where the milk dries
Stem up to 7 cm, paler than the cap, with shallow pits
Abundant white milk, acrid; dirty white flesh turning brown
Mostly with birch, also spruce and pine · summer to autumn

resources.string: Toxic: the DGfM lists it for a gastrointestinal syndrome and a suspected cancer-causing or mutation-causing effect. Wikipedia (en) names a mutagenic substance, necatorin, that boiling reduces but does not remove, and says most western European authorities rate it inedible or poor.

string-array.name: myco_imbricatus_traits
string-array.item: Cap up to 15 cm, brownish to buff, funnel-shaped, with coarse dark scales that turn up with age
Spines instead of gills: soft and pale grey, 0.5 to 1.5 cm, browner with age
Stem pale grey or brown, up to 10 cm, sometimes off-centre
Soft, whitish to tan flesh; can be bitter, especially when old
Brown spore print
With spruce and fir, often in hills and mountains, sometimes in rings · August to October

resources.string: Not recommended: the Swiss controllers (VAPKO) list it only as a seasoning, and Wikipedia (en) calls it edible but not recommended: bitter when old, it can upset the gut. Other mushrooms with spines look alike: Sarcodon amarascens (bitter, with a bluish-black stripe) and Hydnellum scabrosum (bitter, turquoise-tinted base).
Olive slime on a pitted cap

string-array.name: myco_rubellus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 2.5 to 10 cm, conical then with a boss, rust to tawny, finely fibrous, paler at the margin
Gills spaced, ochre or cinnamon, darker with age: true gills, not ridges
Stem 6 to 10 cm, slightly bulbous, the colour of the cap, with yellow veil fragments in the lower half
Pale yellow to saffron flesh, smell of radish
Wet conifer woods (spruce), moss, acid soils · late summer to autumn

resources.string: Deadly: orellanine can severely damage the kidneys after a long symptom-free interval, sometimes lasting days. Thirst, back pain and reduced urine may follow. Dialysis or transplantation is needed in some cases, but outcomes vary. Suspected ingestion is a medical emergency even before symptoms appear.

string-array.name: myco_verna_traits
string-array.item: Pure white cap, 4 to 10 cm, convex to flat, sometimes ivory or ochre at the centre
Gills free, crowded, white
Stem 7 to 13 cm, white and silky, with a rounded bulb
Thin, high membranous ring, sometimes torn or hard to see
Whitish, sac-like volva, 2 to 3 cm
Deciduous or mixed woodland in Europe, mainly spring; similar white amanitas need expert separation

resources.string: Deadly amatoxin-producing amanita. Symptoms may begin many hours after a meal and severe liver injury can follow. Expose the whole stem base to check for the sac-like volva, but the white deadly amanitas cannot be reliably separated by this plate. Seek urgent medical advice after any suspected ingestion.

string-array.name: myco_subincarnata_traits
string-array.item: Small cap about 1.5 to 6 cm, felted to finely scaly, pale rosy-brown to wine pink, darker at the centre
Gills free, fairly crowded, pale cream
Stem about 5 cm and under 1 cm thick, with a faint, fleeting woolly ring zone
Whitish above the ring, scaly below it in the colour of the cap
Odour variable and not a reliable identification test
Hedges, gardens, leaf litter, rich soil

resources.string: Deadly: contains amatoxins that can cause delayed liver failure. It can be confused with small edible grassland mushrooms, including the fairy ring champignon. A faint or missing ring does not make it safe. Suspected ingestion requires urgent medical advice before symptoms appear.
Inocybe à lames couleur de terre

string-array.name: myco_geophylla_traits
string-array.item: Cap 1 to 4 cm, conical, always with a boss, milk-white then slightly ochre, silky
Gills white to cream, then grey, earthy brown with the spores
Slender stem, white, powdery at the top
Strong spermatic smell, acrid flesh
Shady broadleaf woods, sometimes conifers, grass, paths · June to November

resources.string: Toxic: muscarine. Wikipedia (fr) counts it among the most toxic inocybes; the Belgian poison centre describes the sweating syndrome: runny nose, drooling, heavy sweating, tears, breathing difficulty, from a few minutes to 2 hours after the meal; it heals within 24 hours, atropine is sometimes needed. A lilac form exists and has been taken for the amethyst deceiver. The white form is also compared with St George’s mushroom (Wikipedia, en), which is larger, smells of flour and keeps white gills.

string-array.name: myco_sulphureum_traits
string-array.item: Cap up to 8 cm, convex, sulphur-yellow, sometimes brownish at the centre, faint boss
Gills thick, widely spaced, notched
Stem up to 10 cm, bare
Thin flesh; strong smell of coal gas (skatole), nauseating; bitter taste
Deciduous woods, especially beech · spring to autumn
White spore print

resources.string: Toxic: the DGfM lists it for a gastrointestinal syndrome, and Wikipedia (en) calls it inedible and suspected poisonous, with some neurological symptoms reported. Smell and colour tell it from the yellow knight, which is darker, with a sticky cap, white flesh, thin crowded gills and a smell of flour (Wikipedia, en).

string-array.name: myco_citrina_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 10 cm, pale lemon-yellow, sometimes nearly white, with greyish-white patches (volva remains)
Gills white, free
Stem 6 to 12 cm, with an ample, persistent ring, striate above
Bulb with a rim formed by the volva: not a sac
Smell of raw potato or radish
Deciduous and conifer woods, silicate soils · autumn, very common

resources.string: Toxic: the DGfM lists it for a gastrointestinal syndrome, notes bufotenin and warns against eating it raw. Wikipedia (fr) calls it a poor edible, slightly toxic, and says most mycologists advise throwing it away. Its real danger is its resemblance to the death cap, when young and in its yellowish and white forms; the raw-potato smell and the bulb with a rim, not a sac, set it apart.
Yellow veil fragments on the stem

string-array.name: myco_g_knights_points
string-array.item: Yellow knight: darker, sticky cap, white flesh, thin crowded gills, smell of flour. Sulphur knight: sulphur-yellow cap, thick, widely spaced gills, smell of coal gas.
The smell and the colour are what Wikipedia gives to tell them apart.
Neither is to be eaten: the yellow knight is toxic (see its card), the sulphur knight is listed by the DGfM for a gastrointestinal syndrome.

string-array.name: myco_sanguifluus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 12 cm, convex with a sunken centre, sticky, pink-buff to orange, sometimes with grey-green patches where bruised
Gills pale wine-pink, slightly running down the stem
Stem 2 to 5 cm, pinkish-beige, sometimes with brownish or reddish pits
Wine-red milk when cut; flesh brick-red under the cap skin, mild to slightly bitter, almost no smell
Pine woods on chalky soil, mostly southern Europe · September to November

resources.string: Edible: Wikipedia (fr) calls it excellent and some authors the best of the milk caps; the DGfM and the VAPKO list it (red list category 2 in Germany). Wikipedia (en) warns that it can accumulate heavy metals: not from roadsides or polluted ground. The milk is the key: wine-red from the start. Orange milk points to the delicious milk cap or its cousins (see the group). Wikipedia (fr) says the look-alikes share its food safety but not its culinary value.

string-array.name: myco_deterrimus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 12 cm, carrot-orange, sticky, depressed to funnel-shaped, turning green with age, frost or bruising
Gills close, orange then salmon, green-spotted with age
Stem 3 to 8 cm, orange, smooth, without pits, often with a white band at the top
Scarce orange milk turning wine-purple in about half an hour; fruity smell, taste bitter and peppery
Under spruce (also bearberry) · June to November, mostly August to October

resources.string: Edible but mediocre: Wikipedia (fr) and (en) agree on a bitter, unpleasant taste and often maggots; the DGfM and the VAPKO list it. Eating several can turn the urine red, which is harmless (Wikipedia, en). The delicious milk cap grows only under pines, with concentric zones on the cap and pits on the stem; the salmon milk cap grows under firs and does not turn green.

string-array.name: myco_salmonicolor_traits
string-array.item: Cap 6 to 15 cm, funnel-shaped with age, thin concentric rings in orange or paler, never green
Gills orange, crowded, running down the stem
Stem 2 to 10 cm, the colour of the cap, soon hollow, often pitted
Fairly abundant orange milk; flesh orange to red, white in the centre of the stem; fruity smell, taste mild or bitter
Under firs, mostly white fir, on rich soils · mainly autumn

resources.string: Edible, of little interest for some authors (Wikipedia, fr); the VAPKO notes a strong resinous taste, and the DGfM and the VAPKO list it. Under firs and never green: that sets it apart from the false saffron milkcap (under spruce, turning green) and from the delicious milk cap (under pines, mild milk).

string-array.name: myco_luteus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 15 cm, brown to chestnut, very slimy and glossy, the skin peels off
Fine yellow pores, turning olive with age
Stem 4 to 12 cm, pale, with a wide ring: white above, violet-brown below
Glandular dots above the ring
Mild taste, faint pleasant smell
Under pines · mostly autumn

resources.string: Edible: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it. Wikipedia (fr) calls it mediocre, the tastiest of its genus, and advises picking only young ones, peeling the cap and removing the stem; the slimy skin is laxative and may cause indigestion, and allergies are possible. It strongly accumulates caesium-137 (Wikipedia, fr). The granulated bolete has no ring; the larch bolete grows under larches; a young Gomphidius looks alike from above but has gills (Wikipedia, en).

string-array.name: myco_vesca_traits
string-array.item: Cap 5 to 10 cm, pale then pink-ochre, wine-pink or purple-brown, often marbled with olive or rust patches
The skin stops short of the margin, so the gills "show their teeth"
Gills white to cream, close, forked near the stem, rust-spotted with age
Stem 2 to 10 cm, firm, white, sometimes tinged pink, browning at the base
Firm white flesh, mild taste with a nutty note
Under broadleaf trees, especially oaks, on light acid soil · July to October, sometimes from May

resources.string: Good edible (Wikipedia, fr); the DGfM and the VAPKO list it. Rubbing the stem with ferrous sulfate turns it salmon (Wikipedia, en). Wikipedia (fr) names among its look-alikes the charcoal burner and the olive brittlegill (see their cards). The Belgian poison centre names the sickener among the russulas that cause a mild gastrointestinal illness.

string-array.name: myco_rufescens_traits
string-array.item: Cap orange to reddish-orange, russet rather than beige, finely woolly then smooth, wavy margin, often paler
Fine, brittle spines, cream with orange tints, attached to the stem and never running down it
Central stem, thinner than the pied-de-mouton, white to pale pink, turning dark yellow when handled
Brittle white flesh, fruity smell, mild or somewhat bitter taste
Broadleaf and conifer woods, alone or in large rings · July to October

resources.string: Edible, but less prized than the pied-de-mouton: less fleshy and slightly more bitter (Wikipedia, fr); the DGfM and the VAPKO list it. No poisoning is known (Wikipedia, fr). It differs from the pied-de-mouton by its russet cap, its smaller size and its spines that do not run down the stem; intermediate forms exist, so the two are often hard to separate. The size of the cap is not given by the sources read.
Spines do not run down the stem

string-array.name: myco_g_pinebolete_points
string-array.item: Slippery jack: a wide ring, white above and violet-brown below. Granulated bolete: no ring.
Both are slimy-capped boletes of pine woods, with fine yellow pores.
Wikipedia (fr) says the slippery jack is edible with care (peeled cap, young ones only); the granulated bolete has a card of its own, with the more prudent status.
Bovine bolete: no ring either, but very large angular pores running down the stem and a slimmer stem. Slimy spike-cap: gills, not pores, and only an indistinct ring zone (Wikipedia, en).

Velvet bolete: felted, speckled cap, no ring, slightly bluing flesh. Larch bolete: ringed stem, under larches, bright yellow to orange. Olive-brown waxy cap: gills waxy and attached; the slimy spike-cap’s gills separate easily from the cap (Wikipedia, en).

string-array.name: myco_g_hedgehog_points
string-array.item: Pied-de-mouton: beige cap, sturdy, spines running down the stem. Terracotta hedgehog: russet cap, smaller and thinner, spines that do not run down the stem.
Intermediate forms link the two species (Wikipedia, fr): the difference is not always clear.
Both are edible and have spines instead of gills or pores; the terracotta hedgehog is less fleshy and slightly more bitter.

string-array.name: myco_volemus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 5 to 11 cm, apricot to tawny, velvety or smooth, flat with a sunken centre
Gills narrow, very crowded, sometimes forked, pale golden yellow, turning brown when crushed
Stem 4 to 12 cm, firm, slightly paler than the cap
Abundant white milk that turns brownish in the air and stains brown; whitish, firm flesh
Fishy smell, which fades on cooking
Under broadleaf and conifer trees · summer and autumn

resources.string: Edible: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it. Wikipedia (fr) calls its taste mediocre, Wikipedia (en) recommends it for cooking, slowly rather than pan-fried because of the milk. The fishy smell fades on cooking (Wikipedia, en). Wikipedia (en) reports one case of transient pancreatitis in two elderly people in Turkey who had eaten it before. Close species (Lactifluus corrugis, L. rugatus) are hard to tell apart; the sources read give no field rule.

string-array.name: myco_glutinosus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 12 cm, convex then flat, dark brownish to purplish-grey, covered in thick slime
Gills widely spaced, running down the stem, white then grey, blackening with the spores
Stem 4 to 10 cm, white above, yellow at the base; the veil leaves only an indistinct ring zone, stained by the spores
Whitish flesh, faint smell, mild or slightly acidic taste
Under conifers, often spruce · July to November

resources.string: Edible once the slime and the skin of the cap are removed: the DGfM and the VAPKO say so, Wikipedia (fr) calls it honourable or mediocre, Wikipedia (en) says opinions differ and that it accumulates heavy metals. Seen from above a young one looks like the slippery jack, but it has gills, not pores (Wikipedia, en); Wikipedia (fr) names Gomphidius maculatus, under larches, as its main look-alike.

string-array.name: myco_bovinus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 10 cm, sticky, ochre to brownish-yellow, sometimes tinged pink, wavy edge
Very large angular pores, running down the stem, yellow to olive
Stem 3 to 10 cm, slim, beige to ochre, no ring
Soft, elastic, cream flesh, mild taste
Under pines, in groups · July to November

resources.string: Edible but of poor quality: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it; Wikipedia (fr) calls the flesh flabby and tasteless and, like other slippery boletes, laxative for some people; it advises young ones only, the stem removed and the cap peeled. Wikipedia (en) adds that old ones are rubbery and often full of maggots. It has no ring, unlike the slippery jack; the variegated bolete has smaller round pores that blue.

string-array.name: myco_scabrum_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 20 cm, tan to dark brown, smooth or velvety, sticky when wet
Pores whitish then grey, browning when touched
Stem 5 to 20 cm, white, covered in small blackish-brown scales
Whitish flesh, almost unchanging when cut; mild taste, faint smell
Almost only under birch · summer to late autumn

resources.string: Edible when well cooked: the DGfM and the VAPKO list the rough-stemmed boletes, and Wikipedia (fr) warns that raw or undercooked ones cause digestive upset. Of medium value; the fibrous stem is often thrown away, young caps are preferred. The flesh darkens, even turns black, when cooked (Wikipedia, fr and en). The many other rough-stemmed boletes are close; the sources read give no simple rule to separate them.

string-array.name: myco_odora_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 8 cm, bluish to grey-green, fading, frosted, inrolled margin
Gills thin, widely spaced, slightly running down the stem, whitish
Stem fibrous, bent, pale bluish-green, thicker at the base, no ring
Strong sweet smell of aniseed, which stays when dried
Mostly broadleaf woods, sometimes conifers · midsummer to late autumn

resources.string: Not recommended: the sources disagree. The DGfM and the VAPKO list it, Wikipedia (fr) calls it a good edible used mostly as a seasoning, while Wikipedia (en) says edible but not recommended, some guides advising against it, and warns that young ones may be mistaken for the verdigris agaric and other poisonous species. The most prudent status is kept.

string-array.name: myco_piperatus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 6 to 16 cm, dry, creamy-white, staining tan with age, sunken in the centre
Gills very crowded and narrow, running down the stem, white then cream
Stem 2 to 8 cm, white and smooth
Thick, firm white flesh; abundant white milk, very hot and acrid, drying olive-green
Deciduous woods, especially beech · summer to early winter

resources.string: Not recommended: the DGfM lists it with the advice to cook it through thoroughly, but Wikipedia (en) says it contains toxins, that some sources call it inedible or poisonous, and that raw it irritated lips and tongue for about an hour. Boiling removes the bite. The most prudent status is kept. Wikipedia (fr) has no description of the species: the text comes from Wikipedia (en) alone. Do not confuse it with the white Russula delica, which gives no milk.

string-array.name: myco_decastes_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 15 cm, fawn to light brown, sometimes greyish, rolled wavy margin
Gills close, whitish to cream
Stem stocky, white, no ring; stems fused in a clump
Smell floury to fungal, sometimes absent
Edges and paths of woods, especially under poplars · late summer to autumn

resources.string: Not recommended: the sources disagree. The DGfM and the VAPKO list it and Wikipedia (en) calls it edible or choice, but Wikipedia (fr) says some describe it as not to be eaten and others as poorly tolerated, and advises abstaining when in doubt; some gastric upset is reported (Wikipedia, en). The most prudent status is kept. Both pages warn of look-alikes among the entolomas (see the group) and Wikipedia (en) of Clitocybe dilatata.
Yellow pores running down the stem
Small blackish scales on the stem

string-array.name: myco_xerampelina_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 20 cm, wine-red to purple with a carmine edge and a blackish-purple centre, sometimes greenish
Gills nearly free, cream, yellowing with age, with purplish edges
Stem 4 to 12 cm, white, sometimes tinged red, browning when bruised
Smell of boiled crab or shrimp, stronger with age; mild taste
Mostly under conifers, spruce, pine or fir · summer to autumn

resources.string: Edible: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it. Wikipedia (en) counts it among the best edibles of its genus, young caps being good for stuffing; Wikipedia (fr) places it among the edibles but finds its crayfish or herring taste unappealing. The shellfish smell stays when cooked (Wikipedia, en). The sickener has a white stem and white gills (Wikipedia, en): see the group.

string-array.name: myco_nobilis_traits
string-array.item: Cap about 3 to 9 cm, red or rosy, convex then flat, sometimes sticky when wet; the skin peels about a third of the way in
Gills white, crowded
Stem 2 to 5 cm, white, firmer than that of the sickener
White flesh and brittle, chalk-like gills; odour varies and is not diagnostic
Under beech · widespread in Europe

resources.string: Inedible and reported to cause gastrointestinal upset. The German mycological society lists it under its former name Russula mairei. Cap colour or a possible coconut-like odour does not distinguish it reliably from other red brittlegills. Do not eat an uncertain collection.

string-array.name: myco_aurea_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 10 cm, vermilion red shading to orange, with golden-yellow patches, or all golden-yellow; sunken centre, wavy edge
Gills cream then lemon yellow, the edges the most vivid, often forked
Stem 5 to 9 cm, white washed with yellow, lightly striate
Brittle white flesh with a yellow layer under the cap skin; mild, nutty taste
Under broadleaf trees (beech, oak, hazel) · mainly summer

resources.string: Edible: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it; Wikipedia (fr) calls it excellent and says the French agency ANSES supports its sale fresh, dried or canned. Wikipedia (en) warns that it is look-alike to the bloody brittlegill, the sickener and the beechwood sickener, red-capped, peppery and inedible: see the group. Pale forms may be mistaken for the chameleon russula (Wikipedia, fr); only the microscope separates some close species.

string-array.name: myco_versipelle_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 18 cm, ochre-orange to orange-brown, velvety to felty
Pores grey, the same colour as the tubes
Stem 3 to 20 cm, covered with dense black tufts
White flesh turning grey-pink then dark grey-violet when cut; mild taste, faint smell
Under birch · July to November

resources.string: Edible when well cooked: the DGfM lists it and the VAPKO lists the rough-stemmed boletes. Wikipedia (fr) says the fibrous stem is often thrown away and that rough-stemmed boletes upset the stomach if raw or undercooked; Wikipedia (en) calls it mildly toxic unless properly heated (15 to 20 minutes of frying or boiling), with nausea and vomiting. Flesh colour on cutting differs: pink to grey-violet (fr), reddish then brownish (en). It turns black when cooked.

string-array.name: myco_agathosmus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 10 cm, convex with rolled-in edges, dull ashy grey, sticky when moist
Gills white then greyish, running slightly down the stem
Stem 4 to 15 cm, whitish, pale ashy with age, no veil
Soft whitish flesh; strong smell of cherry stones or bitter almonds, bland taste
Under spruce and pine, scattered

resources.string: Edible but bland: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it; Wikipedia (en) is the only page with a description (the French page is a stub). The smell is the mark: Wikipedia (en) names smaller waxy caps with a similar almond smell, which this atlas does not draw.

string-array.name: myco_marzuolus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 2.5 to 12 cm, convex, sticky, pale greyish-brown in the centre and darker, blackish-grey toward the margin
Gills broad, distant, white then grey to bluish-grey
Stem 3 to 10 cm, whitish, greying
Flesh water-soaked under the cap skin, greyish; no noticeable smell or taste
Under conifers, beech, on chalky soil, under melting snow · late winter to early spring, mainly March

resources.string: Edible and well regarded (Wikipedia, fr and en); the DGfM and the VAPKO list it, and the DGfM marks it as protected in Germany and on the red list (category 2). It comes up in winter, when few other mushrooms do. The French page is nearly empty: the description comes from Wikipedia (en).

string-array.name: myco_excoriata_traits
string-array.item: Cap 6 to 10 cm, convex to shield-shaped, brownish raised centre, ochre-yellow to pale brown scales
Gills white to cream, free
Stem 5 to 15 cm, smooth, with a bulbous base and a white ring
White, tender flesh that does not change colour; weak smell, hazelnut taste
Fields, lawns and roadsides · mid-summer to late autumn

resources.string: Edible: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it. Wikipedia (fr) says it is good provided the stem is thrown away; Wikipedia (en) advises eating it young and not gathering it by roadsides, and warns that it looks like many toxic species, which makes picking it risky. It is smaller than the parasol. The French page is a stub: the description comes from Wikipedia (en).
Grey-brown cap, darker at the margin

string-array.name: myco_g_redrussula_points
string-array.item: Gilded brittlegill (edible): cream gills turning lemon-yellow, often forked, stem washed with yellow, mild nutty taste.
Sickener and beechwood sickener (toxic): white gills and white stem, peppery taste; the DGfM lists both for a gastrointestinal syndrome.
Shrimp russula (edible): wine-purple cap, gills cream then yellowing, smell of crab or shrimp. Wikipedia (en) says the sickener always has a white stem and white gills.

Wikipedia (en) lists the sickener and the beechwood sickener as look-alikes of the gilded brittlegill; the sources read give no further field rule, and some close species are separated only by the microscope.
Russula paludosa: blood red, pink or purple cap, crowded cream-then-yellow gills; Wikipedia (en) says it is easily mistaken for the sickener, which is poisonous.

string-array.name: myco_g_roughstem_points
string-array.item: Birch bolete: tan to dark brown cap, whitish flesh almost unchanging. Orange birch bolete: ochre-orange cap, flesh turning grey-violet, stem covered with dense black tufts.
Both grow under birch and have a stem covered with dark scales.
Both must be well cooked: raw or undercooked rough-stemmed boletes upset the stomach (Wikipedia, fr). Other rough-stemmed boletes exist, and the sources read give no simple rule to separate them all.

Orange oak bolete: brick-red cap, scales turning white, reddish, then black, flesh turning grey-violet, under oaks (Wikipedia, fr). Cracked bolete: cracked cap, yellow pores and stem, fine yellowish scales (Wikipedia, fr).

string-array.name: myco_gemmata_traits
string-array.item: Cap 2.5 to 12 cm, creamy to golden yellow, sticky when moist, with soft white plaques that rain washes off
Gills white, closely spaced
Stem 4 to 12 cm, pale, with a flimsy ring that is easily lost
White volva forming a small free rim at the base
Sandy, slightly acid soil, near conifers · spring to autumn

resources.string: Toxic: the DGfM lists it as suspect, with the panther cap syndrome, and Wikipedia (en) gives ibotenic acid and muscimol, with symptoms within three hours (hallucinations, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain), severe cases being extremely rare. Wikipedia (fr) says it causes the same symptoms as the panther cap and the fly agaric. Wikipedia (en) names the false death cap, Amanita fulva (the tawny grisette) and the panther cap as look-alikes; its cap is brighter yellow than the first.

string-array.name: myco_porphyria_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 10 cm, brown with a purplish or greyish tint, sometimes with grey veil patches
Gills whitish, free, darkening when bruised
Stem 5 to 12 cm, bulbous base, with a fragile grey-violet or blackened ring
Base sometimes in a white membranous volva
White flesh with a smell of raw potato or radish
Poor soil, mostly under conifers (spruce) · summer to autumn

resources.string: Toxic: the DGfM lists it for a gastrointestinal syndrome, notes bufotenin and warns against eating it raw; Wikipedia (en) calls it inedible. It looks like the false death cap in shape and smell but differs in cap colour and ring colour, and is easily mistaken for the death cap, which is far more poisonous (Wikipedia, en). It can also be taken for the panther cap. It has no French Wikipedia page: the text comes from Wikipedia (en) and the DGfM.

string-array.name: myco_moelleri_traits
string-array.item: Cap 5 to 15 cm, covered in small dark grey to grey-brown scales on a pale background, yellowing when touched
Gills free, grey-pink when young, then brown
Stem 6 to 12 cm, clearly bulbous, with a thin white ring; the base yellows strongly when handled
White flesh, chrome-yellow at the base of the stem; strong smell of phenol, iodoform or ink
Broadleaf woods, mostly on chalky soil, also parks and meadows

resources.string: Toxic: Wikipedia (fr) says so plainly, the DGfM lists it for a gastrointestinal syndrome, and Wikipedia (en) says that like the yellow stainer it upsets some people and not others. The yellowing and the carbolic smell are what warn. It is not the field mushroom: see the group.

string-array.name: myco_clavipes_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 8 cm, convex then flat or dished, grey-brown sometimes olive, paler margin
Gills cream-yellow, strongly running down the stem, some forked
Stem 3 to 7 cm, silky, the colour of the cap, with a markedly bulbous, club-shaped base
Thick white flesh, slightly yellow at the base; faint, watery, sweetish smell
Conifer and broadleaf woods, especially beech · August to November

resources.string: Not recommended: never with alcohol. The DGfM lists it as harmless without alcohol and gives the coprine-type syndrome with it; Wikipedia (en) describes a reaction 5 to 10 minutes after drinking (flushing, throbbing in the head and neck, puffy hands) and says it is edible but unpalatable, some sources listing it inedible. There is no French Wikipedia page: the text comes from Wikipedia (en) and the DGfM. Wikipedia (en) separates it from the clouded agaric by its club-shaped stem.

string-array.name: myco_helvus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 15 cm, velvety, funnel-shaped with age, beige to light grey at the margin and darker at the centre
Gills cream then ochre-yellow, running down the stem
Stem 3 to 9 cm, hollow, whitish then ochre or pink-tinged
Watery, colourless milk; white or beige flesh, often pink-tinged
Strong smell of fenugreek, lovage or celery; mild taste
Wet places, often among sphagnum, near spruce, pine and birch · late summer and autumn

resources.string: Toxic: the DGfM lists it for a gastrointestinal syndrome, and Wikipedia (en) calls it mildly toxic raw, with nausea, vomiting, vertigo and chills within 30 minutes, the toxins being destroyed by thorough boiling; 418 people were poisoned near Leipzig in October 1949. The dried mushroom is used as a spice in small amounts. The French Wikipedia page is a stub: the description comes from Wikipedia (en).

string-array.name: myco_platyphylla_traits
string-array.item: Cap 5 to 12 cm, ash-grey, olive or grey-brown, darker at the centre, with radial fibrils, often split at the edge
Gills broad and deep, whitish then cream, nearly free, edges serrated
Stem 5 to 12 cm, fibrous and tough, paler than the cap, with white cords at the base
Thin, whitish flesh; mild to slightly bitter taste, no distinctive smell
Rotting broadleaf wood, also beechnuts in the soil · late spring to autumn

resources.string: Toxic: the DGfM lists it for a gastrointestinal syndrome, and Wikipedia (fr) says it was eaten in Italy, mixed with other species, despite its bitterness, and is now considered toxic. Wikipedia (fr) names look-alikes among Pluteus cervinus, Hymenopellis radicata and Tricholoma portentosum; the thin flesh, broad soft gills and white cords help set it apart. There is no English page read: the text comes from Wikipedia (fr) and the DGfM.

string-array.name: myco_fusipes_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 10 cm, convex to conical, slightly nippled, reddish-brown and paler at the centre
Gills spaced, whitish-pink, staining rusty red
Stem 8 to 14 cm, swollen in the middle and tapering at both ends, rooting, deeply grooved, reddish-brown to blackish below, no ring
Firm whitish flesh, mild sweet taste
In clumps on broadleaf stumps, mostly oak · summer to autumn

resources.string: Toxic: the DGfM lists it for a gastrointestinal syndrome. The sources read disagree: Wikipedia (fr) calls it fairly good if only very young caps are eaten, with the tough stem removed, and warns that late harvests cause indigestion; Wikipedia (en) says most authors do not think it worth a meal and that old ones risk gastro-enteritis. The most prudent status, the DGfM one, is kept. Wikipedia (fr) says beginners may take it for a pholiota, a hypholoma or an honey fungus; it has no ring and a grooved spindle stem.

string-array.name: myco_conica_traits
string-array.item: Cap up to 10 cm, narrowly conical then umbonate and often lobed, yellow to orange or scarlet, viscid when young
Gills waxy, white to pale yellow or greyish
Stem up to 20 cm, fibrillose, yellow to orange-red, whitish at the base, no ring
Yellowish flesh; every part greys with age and finally turns black
Waxcap grassland, dunes, road verges · summer and autumn

resources.string: Toxic: the DGfM lists it for a gastrointestinal syndrome. Wikipedia (en) says its edibility is unknown and that it may be poisonous, quoting Arora: reported poisonings may come from other species, and it may cause minor effects such as lightheadedness. There is no French Wikipedia page: the text comes from Wikipedia (en) and the DGfM. The most prudent status is kept.

string-array.name: myco_g_cloudy_points
string-array.item: Club foot: a markedly bulbous, club-shaped stem, deeply running gills, a grey-brown cap, often olive-tinged. Clouded agaric: darker overall (Wikipedia, en).
The club foot is harmless without alcohol and causes a flushing reaction with it; the clouded agaric is judged inconsistently, the DGfM noting a suspicion of carcinogenicity or mutagenicity.
Neither has a card that says to eat it.

string-array.name: myco_castanea_traits
string-array.item: Cap up to 3 cm, broadly bell-shaped to flat, white with dark red-brown scales
Gills whitish
Stem up to 8 cm, typically chestnut-brown, with an indistinct ring
Whitish flesh, mild taste
Coniferous and deciduous woods, alone or in small groups

resources.string: Deadly: the sources disagree on the cause. Wikipedia (en) says it contains amatoxins, potentially deadly for the liver; the DGfM lists it under the death-cap syndrome but notes that more recent findings show no amatoxins; Wikipedia (fr) calls it moderately toxic and advises against eating it. The most prudent status is kept. The DGfM warns that small lepiotas with brownish and red pigments are suspected of containing amatoxins; the Belgian poison centre advises against any lepiota under 10 cm. The French Wikipedia page is a stub: the description comes from Wikipedia (en).

string-array.name: myco_maculatum_traits
string-array.item: Cap up to 8 cm, conical or bell-shaped then with a broad boss, fibrous, chestnut-brown and paler at the margin, which is usually split; white veil remnants in the centre when young
Gills crowded, greyish-white then olive-brown, with finely toothed white edges
Stem up to 8 cm, cream turning browner, often thicker at the base, solid then hollow
White flesh, mild taste, strong pungent fruity smell
Broadleaf or mixed woods, at the foot of trees, especially beech, on chalky soil · spore print snuff brown

resources.string: Toxic: muscarine (the DGfM and Wikipedia, en). Symptoms: salivation, tears, urination, diarrhoea, digestive upset and vomiting; death by respiratory failure is possible (Wikipedia, en). It has no French Wikipedia page: the text comes from Wikipedia (en) and the DGfM. Wikipedia (en) names look-alikes among other inocybes (Inocybe lacera, I. lanatodisca, I. fastigiata).

string-array.name: myco_rosea_traits
string-array.item: Cap 2 to 6 cm, bright to pale pink, with a small boss and a striate margin
Gills adnate or notched, pale pink to white
Stem very brittle, white with pink tints
Smell of radish
Edges of broadleaf woods

resources.string: Toxic: muscarine (the DGfM and Wikipedia, fr), with sweating, nausea and vomiting. Wikipedia (en) lists it as poisonous without naming a toxin. It is a close relative of Mycena sororia, separable only with the microscope (Wikipedia, en).

string-array.name: myco_micaceus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 6 cm, ovoid then bell-shaped, tawny or yellow-ochre, darker at the centre, with shiny mica-like granules when young
Gills close, white then brownish then black, dissolving from the edge
Stem 5 to 10 cm, whitish, hollow and fragile, no ring
Thin white flesh; no distinctive smell or taste
In clusters on stumps and rotting wood · spring to early winter

resources.string: Not recommended with alcohol: the DGfM lists it for the coprine syndrome while noting only small amounts of coprine; Wikipedia (fr) says European harvests may cause mild excitation with alcohol, less than the common ink cap; Wikipedia (en) says it has no coprine. Both pages call it edible when young, before the gills dissolve, though of little interest. The most prudent status is kept. Wikipedia (en) advises against roadside harvests (heavy metals) and separates it from the common ink cap, which is larger, grey and without glistening granules.

string-array.name: myco_regalis_traits
string-array.item: Cap 10 to 25 cm, yellowish-brown, with ochre warts in rings; the skin peels almost to the centre
Gills crowded, free, white with a creamy tint
Stem 10 to 20 cm, with a ring and a bulb ringed with small yellow-ochre warts
Whitish flesh, golden-yellow under the cap skin; no notable smell or taste
Mountain woods under birch, pine and spruce; rare · Scandinavia and eastern Europe

resources.string: Toxic: same toxins as the fly agaric (ibotenic acid and muscimol), which cooking does not remove; the DGfM lists it for the panther cap syndrome. Wikipedia (en) reports three people in Finland who ate it for a parasol and had digestive, nervous and cholinergic symptoms, recovered within 4 to 24 hours. Wikipedia (fr) only says it looks like the fly agaric without its colour and is also toxic. Wikipedia (en) separates it from the blusher (stains pink, white flesh under the skin) and the panther cap (white flesh under the skin, cup-shaped bulb).

string-array.name: myco_asperum_traits
string-array.item: Cap up to 10 cm, reddish-brown at the centre, breaking into erect pyramidal scales on a paler ground
Gills white, free, crowded, tending to fork
Stem about 10 cm, paler, with sparse brown scales below a large cottony ring
White flesh, said to smell of rubber
Deciduous woods, parks and gardens with wood-chip mulch · autumn

resources.string: Toxic: the DGfM lists it for the coprinus-type syndrome with alcohol, from unknown inhibitors of the alcohol-breakdown enzyme (no coprine); Wikipedia (en) says it is not recommended, linked to alcohol intolerance and possibly poisonous, and that it looks like amanitas, some of them deadly. It has no French Wikipedia page: the text comes from Wikipedia (en) and the DGfM.
Cream stem, thicker at the base

string-array.name: myco_g_smalllepiota_points
string-array.item: Deadly parasol, fatal dapperling and chestnut dapperling are all small lepiotas, with brownish or red scales or pigments; the DGfM lists all three for the death-cap syndrome.
Chestnut dapperling: up to 3 cm, white cap with dark red-brown scales, chestnut-brown stem, indistinct ring (Wikipedia, en).
The DGfM suspects every small lepiota with brownish and red pigments of containing amatoxins; the Belgian poison centre advises against any lepiota under 10 cm.

string-array.name: myco_semisanguifluus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 2.5 to 7 cm, sticky, pinkish-beige or greyish-brown, sometimes lilac-tinged, with distinct zones; it turns green very quickly
Gills salmon-orange to brownish-orange
Stem 3 to 5 cm, greyish orange-pink, greening when handled, few or no pits
Orange to reddish-orange flesh; scarce orange-red milk turning wine-red in 5 to 8 minutes, then brownish-red
Mild or slightly peppery taste, faint smell
Only under pines, on chalky soil, often in grass; uncommon

resources.string: Edible: Wikipedia (fr) calls it a good edible, the DGfM lists it (red list category 3 in Germany) and so does the VAPKO. Wikipedia (fr) separates it from the false saffron milkcap (under spruce, stem without pits, strongly greening cap) and from the delicious milk cap (brighter colours, milk staying orange); the page also names Lactarius fennoscandicus, very close and under spruce. The milk turning wine-red in minutes is what sets it apart.

string-array.name: myco_grevillei_traits
string-array.item: Cap 2 to 15 cm, sticky, lemon-yellow to bright orange or reddish-brown
Fine yellow pores running down the stem, olive-yellow with age
Stem 3 to 12 cm, yellow above a white then yellow ring, orange-reddish brown at the base
Soft bright yellow flesh, quickly turning cream with orange spots; mild, sweet taste
Only under larches · summer to late autumn

resources.string: Edible but mediocre: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it, the VAPKO adding that the cap skin must be removed. Wikipedia (fr) finds it bland and flabby and says it can be laxative for some; it advises young ones only, the stem removed, the cap peeled and a small first portion. It is hard to mix up thanks to its colours, its ringed stem and the larches (Wikipedia, fr): the other slippery boletes under larches have large pores.

string-array.name: myco_variegatus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 5 to 15 cm, dull yellow to ochre or rusty, felted and speckled with small scales, barely sticky
Fairly large pores, ochre then olive-brown
Stem 4 to 12 cm, nearly smooth, the colour of the cap or paler, no ring
Cream to yellowish flesh, which may turn slightly blue near the tubes; chlorine-like smell and taste
Only under pines, on sandy soil poor in lime

resources.string: Edible but mediocre: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it. Wikipedia (fr) finds the flesh flabby, the chlorine smell passing into the dish, and says it can be laxative; it advises young firm ones, the stem removed, the cap peeled and a small first portion. It strongly accumulates caesium-137 and metals (Wikipedia, fr). The bovine bolete has a plain, paler cap and a slimmer stem (Wikipedia, fr). Wikipedia (en) calls its smell and taste unpleasant.

string-array.name: myco_olivaceoalbus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 12 cm, olive-brown to grey or sooty-brown, slimy, with dark streaks and a persistent dark boss
Gills thick, widely spaced, white, waxy
Stem 3 to 12 cm, slimy when wet, white above a ring-like zone, with ragged dark scaly bands below
Thin white flesh, no distinct smell, bland taste
Under conifers, in mountain woods, on acid ground · late summer to early winter

resources.string: Edible, with divided opinions on taste: the DGfM lists it; Wikipedia (en) says some remove the cap skin, advises caution, and that it is eaten more in Europe than in North America. The page says there is no risk of confusion with toxic fungi, and lists other waxy caps as look-alikes (Hygrophorus latitabundus, H. pustulatus, H. persoonii under oaks). It has no French Wikipedia page: the text comes from Wikipedia (en) and the DGfM.

string-array.name: myco_hypothejus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 6 cm, yellowish to olive-brown with a dark centre, slimy, funnel-shaped with age
Gills yellow, running down the stem
Stem 4 to 7 cm, slender, bare
Pale yellow flesh turning orange-red when bruised
In pine woods, often in large groups · October and November, with the first frosts

resources.string: Edible, of variable quality because some are slimy: the DGfM lists it and Wikipedia (en) says so. Wikipedia (en) names the slimy spike-cap as a look-alike: its gills separate easily from the cap, unlike the waxy gills of this species. It has no French Wikipedia page: the text comes from Wikipedia (en) and the DGfM.

string-array.name: myco_fragrans_traits
string-array.item: Cap 1 to 5 cm, white and flat
Gills somewhat close, running down the stem, whitish
Stem 2 to 6 cm, thin, bare
Fragrant smell of aniseed
Broadleaf woods in Europe · August to December

resources.string: Toxic: the DGfM lists it for the muscarine syndrome. Wikipedia (en) gives it as edible but not recommended, some guides advising against it because it can be mistaken for deadly poisonous species, and names Clitocybe dealbata (the ivory funnel, deadly, with no aniseed smell) and the blue-green anise mushroom as look-alikes. The most prudent status is kept. It has no French Wikipedia page: the text comes from Wikipedia (en) and the DGfM.

string-array.name: myco_chalciporus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 1.5 to 9 cm, dry or slightly sticky, brownish-yellow to brownish-red
Pores slightly angular, rust-brown to reddish-brown
Stem 3 to 9 cm, red-brown over yellow, with yellow mycelium at the base, no ring
Cream flesh, bright yellow at the base of the stem; distinctly peppery taste
Under broadleaf and conifer trees · July to November

resources.string: Not recommended: the VAPKO lists it, but Wikipedia (fr) says it has no food interest because of its peppery taste, and Wikipedia (en) says it is usually considered inedible and contains toxins, advising thorough cooking to reduce the risk of stomach upset. It can serve as a condiment, finely diced or dried and powdered (Wikipedia, fr). The false peppery bolete (Chalciporus pseudopiperatus) is a cryptic species: only DNA tells them apart.
Yellow gills running down the stem
Aniseed funnel: edible, toxic or deadly?

string-array.name: myco_g_anise_points
string-array.item: Blue-green anise mushroom: blue-green frosted cap, strong aniseed smell; listed edible by the DGfM and the VAPKO, but not recommended here.
Clitocybe fragrans: small, white and flat, also smelling of aniseed; the DGfM lists it for the muscarine syndrome.

Fool’s funnel: white to cream, floury smell, no aniseed smell; the DGfM lists it for the muscarine syndrome too. Wikipedia (en) says the ivory funnel (Clitocybe dealbata) is deadly and lacks the aniseed odour.
The DGfM lists Clitocybe dealbata, C. fragrans, C. rivulosa and C. suaveolens for the muscarine syndrome.

string-array.name: myco_integra_traits
string-array.item: Cap 6 to 15 cm, shiny, usually brown with violet, purple, yellow or green tints, nearly spherical then flat or depressed
Gills thin, well spaced, crumbly, white then bright yellow
Stem 5 to 12 cm, thick and white, spotted yellow or rusty with age
Very firm white flesh, mild sweet taste, crunchy
Scattered under conifers, often mountain spruce and fir woods

resources.string: Not recommended: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it, and it is widely eaten in northern Europe and good when young (Wikipedia). But Wikipedia (en) lists it as not recommended, and both pages quote an 1878 study saying poisonings were once frequent: long cooking removes the toxic properties, quick methods such as roasting do not. The most prudent status is kept. Similar species of unknown edibility look like it; Wikipedia (en) names Russula mustelina.

string-array.name: myco_paludosa_traits
string-array.item: Cap 6 to 20 cm, convex to depressed, mostly blood red, pink, crimson or purple, sometimes with a yellowish or orange centre
Gills crowded, cream then yellow, sometimes reddish at the edges
Stem 5 to 15 cm, white, sometimes tinged pink, slightly club-shaped
White flesh, mild taste, no smell, soon soft and greyish
Coniferous woods and peat bogs, especially under pines; locally very common

resources.string: Edible: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it, and Wikipedia (en) says it is a common sight in Finnish markets. Wikipedia (en) warns that it can easily be mistaken for the sickener, which is poisonous: see the group. It has no French Wikipedia page and no English common name: the text comes from Wikipedia (en) and the DGfM.

string-array.name: myco_decolorans_traits
string-array.item: Cap up to 15 cm, red to orange, sticky when moist, convex to flat or depressed
Gills pale, turning yellowish, sometimes staining greyish
Stem up to 12 cm, bare
White flesh that blackens when bruised; mild taste and smell
Mixed woods and under conifers, alone or in groups

resources.string: Edible: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it. Wikipedia (en) advises against eating wild ones because of look-alikes of unknown edibility, without naming them; its flesh blackens when bruised. The red cap and the blackening are what the page gives. It has no French Wikipedia page: the text comes from Wikipedia (en) and the DGfM; the page is short.

string-array.name: myco_aurantiacum_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 15 cm, velvety, brick-red to orange-brown, the skin often overhanging the tubes
Pores whitish then ochre to ochre-brown
Stem 8 to 16 cm, covered in scales that turn from white to reddish and then black
White flesh turning blue-grey, then greyish-violet, then blackish when cut; mild taste, faint smell
Under broadleaf trees, especially oaks

resources.string: Edible when thoroughly cooked: the DGfM lists it (as Leccinum quercinum, with this name as synonym). Wikipedia (fr) calls it good, throws away the fibrous stem and keeps young caps, and warns that raw or undercooked it upsets the stomach; Wikipedia (en) says it must be cooked thoroughly, not parboiled, that Leccinum species are considered by some possibly unsafe and that one death has been linked to this species. Look-alikes under other trees: Leccinum albostipitatum (poplars, white scales), L. versipelle (birches), L. vulpinum and L. piceinum (pines and spruces, no food interest).

string-array.name: myco_cinereus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 2 to 6 cm, funnel-shaped with a hole in the centre, black when young then greyish-black, very lobed edge
Folds, not true gills: decurrent, often joined, bluish-grey then grey
Stem 2 to 5 cm, hollow, curved and grooved, fan-shaped under the folds
Very thin, black, elastic flesh; mild taste, faint smell of mirabelle plum
Broadleaf woods, chestnut groves, chalky soil · late summer to autumn

resources.string: Edible: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it; Wikipedia (fr) calls it well regarded and says the flesh withstands long cooking, Wikipedia (en) that it is milder than the horn of plenty. The horn of plenty is hollow and horn-shaped with a smooth underside; the false chanterelle of the charcoal burners (Faerberia carbonaria) is paler, with a solid stem and true gills, on burnt ground and with no food value (Wikipedia, fr).

string-array.name: myco_pruinatus_traits
string-array.item: Cap 4 to 12 cm, dry or velvety, brownish to blackish, often mauve near the edge, little cracked
Pores the colour of the tubes, golden-yellow then olive-yellow, bluish when pressed
Stem 3 to 10 cm, bright yellow when young, turning reddish to red, bruising blue easily
Firm bright yellow flesh, weakly bluing, slowly; mild sweet taste
Under conifers and broadleaf trees, mostly beech, on acid soils · September to November

resources.string: Edible after cooking: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it; Wikipedia (fr) advises removing the stem and choosing young firm ones. Look-alikes (Wikipedia, fr): the red-cracking bolete (usually a reddish zone in the flesh and no bluing), the bay bolete (no red or mauve, brown stem), the cisalpine bolete (no food interest), Hortiboletus engelii. The English page is nearly empty: the text comes from Wikipedia (fr) and the lists.

string-array.name: myco_rubellus_b_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 12 cm, felted, bright red and paler at the edge, finely cracked when mature
Pores yellow then olive-yellow, usually bluish when bruised
Stem 3 to 10 cm, yellow or red, often bulbous; small red or orange dots at the very base
Whitish to pale yellow flesh, sometimes slightly bluish under the cap; mild taste
Under broadleaf trees, in parks, gardens, clearings and roadsides, on chalky soil

resources.string: Not recommended: the DGfM lists it and Wikipedia (fr) calls it edible after cooking, young firm ones with the stem removed, but to be avoided in urban areas where it absorbs pollutants; Wikipedia (en) says edible but often maggoty, poor, listed as not recommended and its edibility questioned. The most prudent status is kept. Wikipedia (fr) separates it from several small boletes of no food interest, Xerocomellus ripariellus and X. redeuilhii among them.

string-array.name: myco_crocipodium_traits
string-array.item: Cap brown, yellow-brown to cinnamon, velvety, often cracked or tessellated at maturity
Pores small, sulphur yellow to beige, turning olive and ochre-brown when pressed
Stem fusoid, ribbed, whitish to sulphur yellow, with fine yellowish to orange scales
Whitish flesh turning pinkish or salmon, then reddish-violet and blackish when cut; mild or sweet taste
Under oaks, sometimes beech · June to September

resources.string: Edible when cooked: the DGfM lists it. Wikipedia (fr) calls its edibility medium, says the fibrous stem is thrown away and only young caps kept, and warns of stomach upset if raw or undercooked. Look-alikes (Wikipedia, fr): Leccinellum pseudoscabrum (whitish pores), L. lepidum and L. corsicum (darker caps, autumn and winter, edible) and the Butyriboletus, taken for it because of the stem network. The English page is nearly empty: the description comes from Wikipedia (fr).
Shiny brown cap with violet tints
Flesh pink, then violet, then black

string-array.name: myco_g_redbolete_points
string-array.item: Matte bolete: dry dark cap with mauve edge, pores bluing, stem yellow turning red. Ruby bolete: bright red felted cap, small red dots at the stem base. Red-cracking bolete: usually a reddish zone in the flesh and no bluing. Bay bolete: brown stem, no red or mauve (Wikipedia, fr).
The sources read separate them by small features and name several look-alikes of no food interest; they are not told apart by a single rule.
Edibility differs: the bay bolete is good, the red-cracking and matte boletes are edible after cooking, the ruby bolete is not recommended here.

resources.string: Horn of plenty, or ashen chanterelle?

string-array.name: myco_g_blacktrumpet_points
string-array.item: Horn of plenty: horn-shaped, hollow, smooth grey underside. Ashen chanterelle: funnel with a hole, well-formed decurrent folds, bluish-grey then grey (Wikipedia, fr).
Both are black and edible; the ashen chanterelle is milder (Wikipedia, en).
The false chanterelle of the charcoal burners is paler, with a solid stem and true gills, grows on burnt ground and has no food value (Wikipedia, fr).

string-array.name: myco_sordida_traits
string-array.item: Cap light violet, lilac-pink or lilac, smooth, a little greasy in wet weather
Gills notched and crowded, blue like the cap
Stem cylindrical, straight, smooth and fibrillose, no bulb, no ring
Light woods of broadleaf trees and conifers, garden grass, parks, meadows, lawns, roadsides · September to December

resources.string: Edible: the DGfM and the VAPKO list it (the DGfM marks it as on the German red list). Wikipedia (fr) gives no verdict of its own and names the blewits it is mistaken for, all edible: the wood blewit, with a blue stem, and the field blewit, with a violet stem; this one has a straight stem with no bulb. It also names a violet Cortinarius (Cortinarius azureus) among the look-alikes, which is not in this atlas: purple gills alone do not identify a blewit. Wikipedia (en) is a stub with no description, so the text follows the French page; sizes, flesh and spore print are not given there, and the drawing only shows typical shapes.

string-array.name: myco_pulmonarius_traits
string-array.item: Cap 5 to over 20 cm, convex then flat, much paler and smaller than the oyster mushroom
Gills whitish, decurrent
Stem short, off-centre or missing, no ring
Spore print white to greyish or lilac · pleasant anise smell (Wikipedia, en)
On dead wood, mostly broadleaf; later in summer than the oyster mushroom, preferring warmer weather

resources.string: Edible: the DGfM lists it; Wikipedia (fr) and (en) say its taste and cultivation are much the same as the oyster mushroom, and that it is the most cultivated mushroom of this kind in Europe and North America. Wikipedia (en) warns that clitocybes growing on wood can look like it and that some are poisonous; it also says the sold “Pleurotus sajor-caju” is a different mushroom with a ring. Neither page names a danger from the species itself. The atlas draws it as the oyster mushroom, only paler.

string-array.name: myco_sublateritium_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3.5 to 10 cm, brick-red in the centre with a paler margin, smooth, sometimes with veil remnants at the edge
Gills crowded, yellowish or sulphur-yellow at first, greyish with age, never green
Stem light yellow, darker towards the base
Spore print purple-brown · mild nutty taste, a little bitter when old
In dense clusters on stumps and rotting broadleaf wood, in autumn

resources.string: Not recommended: the sources disagree. Wikipedia (fr) calls it toxic, edible after cooking and inedible in the same page; Wikipedia (en) says it is sometimes eaten, a choice edible in Japan, but often thought inedible or poisonous in Europe, and warns against mixing it up with deadly look-alikes, naming the funeral bell. The VAPKO only warns that the sulphur tuft can be confused with it, and it is absent from the DGfM lists. Kept at the most prudent edible status. It differs from the sulphur tuft by its brick-red cap and gills that are never green; the funeral bell is in the group below.

string-array.name: myco_g_blewit_points
string-array.item: Wood blewit: lilac cap, violet gills, a swollen base to the stem. Sordid blewit: straight stem with no bulb, light violet to lilac cap, blue gills.
Wikipedia (fr) says the blewits it is mistaken for are all edible, but names a violet Cortinarius among the look-alikes: a violet colour alone is not enough.
Both are in the DGfM list of edible mushrooms.
